subject: Banking
title: Paper Money from China
description: A fast breakdown of Paper Money from China for builders.

hook.text: China invented paper money in the 7th century. Merchants tired of carrying heavy coins started using receipts instead.

buildup.text: These receipts were IOUs backed by coin deposits. You could trade the paper and claim the coins later.

discovery.text: The Song Dynasty formalized this. Government-issued paper notes became official currency, backed by state reserves.

twist.text: The Yuan Dynasty printed so much paper money it caused hyperinflation. China abandoned paper currency for centuries.

climax.text: Paper money proved that convenience can outrun trust. Print too much and the system collapses.

punchline.text: China invented paper money, then broke it by overprinting.

quiz.question: Why did early Chinese paper money ultimately fail?
options: The government overprinted and caused hyperinflation

details.summary: China invented paper money during the Tang Dynasty around the 7th century, with the Song Dynasty issuing government-backed banknotes called jiaozi by the 10th century, over 600 years before Europe adopted the concept.
details.whyItMatters: Paper money was one of the most consequential financial innovations in history. China's early experiment also provided the first lessons in hyperinflation when the Yuan Dynasty printed too much of it.
takeaways: Chinese merchants created the first paper money as deposit receipts
The Song Dynasty issued official government banknotes around 1024 CE
Overprinting by the Yuan Dynasty caused one of history's first hyperinflations

faq.question: Why didn't paper money spread from China to Europe sooner?
faq.answer: Limited trade connections and cultural differences in monetary trust kept the innovation localized. Marco Polo described Chinese paper money with astonishment, but European nations did not adopt it for centuries.

faq.question: What lessons did China's early paper money teach?
faq.answer: The Yuan Dynasty's hyperinflation proved that paper money requires fiscal discipline to maintain trust. Printing unlimited notes destroys their value, a lesson that governments have relearned repeatedly throughout history.
